proposition: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, the sum of k^3 for k = 1..n equals (n(n+1)/2)^2 + floor(n/6).
hypotheses: the sum is empty for n = 0

argument.text: There is a integer n with 1 <= n <= 60 for which n^2 > 30.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, n^2 is at least n.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, (n-4)*(2*n^2) equals (n-4)*((2*n^2) + [n = 4]).
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, 2*n^2 is congruent to (2*n^2) + 1235 modulo 13.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, at least one of the following holds: n mod 4 = 0; n mod 4 = 1; n mod 4 = 2; n mod 4 = 3.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, (n-3)*(n^2) equals (n-3)*((n^2) + [n = 3]).
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, if n mod 2 = 1 then (n^2) mod 2 = 1.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, if n mod 4 = 0 then (n*(n+1)/2) mod 2 = 0.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, 2*n is at least n.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, n*(n+1) is congruent to (n*(n+1)) + 5083 modulo 221.
At n = 1, the sum of k^3 for k = 1..n = 1.
There is a integer n with 1 <= n <= 60 for which n^3 > 20.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, at least one of the following holds: n mod 2 = 0; n mod 2 = 1.
The steps above establish the statement up to 60, and it is taken to hold for the whole range up to 60.
